⚖️ There's one principle that holds British justice together, and it's carved above the Old Bailey: justice is blind. The law shouldn't care who you are, what you believe, or what colour your rosette is. Treat two people who do the same thing differently, and you haven't bent the rules — you've broken the whole thing.

And a growing number of people no longer believe that promise is being kept. Before anyone calls that a conspiracy — remember the government agreed, and had to pass a law.

⚖️ Last year the Sentencing Council proposed that an offender's ethnic, cultural or religious background should help decide how their sentence was approached. It was branded "two-tier justice." The guidance was pulled the day before it took effect, and Parliament legislated (the Sentencing Guidelines (Pre-Sentence Reports) Act 2025) to ban personal characteristics like race and religion from being used that way.

The system got so close to formally building different tiers into sentencing that the state had to stop it by law. This isn't an internet myth. It's something the government itself admitted was real.

👮 And nothing tests public faith more than how we treat assaults on the police. An attack on an officer is an attack on the thin line between order and chaos. If people come to believe the consequences depend on who you are or what cause you claim, respect for the uniform erodes — and every officer is left a little less safe.

Reform UK: one law, for everyone, blind to politics and background. Keep personal characteristics out of sentencing for good, make assaults on police carry real consequences, and rebuild the confidence equal justice depends on.

Justice must not only be done. It must be seen to be done — by everyone.
